chapters.title: Witnesses to the Earth
chapters.teaser: Jesus gives the disciples a geographic outline that becomes the whole book's roadmap.
body: "Ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth" (v.8) isn't just a farewell blessing — it's a table of contents. Acts moves in exactly that order: Jerusalem dominates the early chapters, Samaria opens up in chapter 8, and the story ends with Paul preaching in Rome itself.

The disciples are still thinking politically — "wilt thou at this time restore again the kingdom to Israel?" (v.6) — and Jesus redirects their question about timing into a commission about mission instead.

chapters.title: Why Stand Ye Gazing Up?
chapters.teaser: Two men in white interrupt the disciples' skyward stare with a promise and a gentle rebuke.
body: As Jesus ascends into a cloud, the disciples are left staring upward until two unnamed men in white ask, essentially, why they're still looking at the sky (v.10-11). Their message pairs comfort with redirection: "this same Jesus... shall so come in like manner as ye have seen him go."
It's a small but pointed scene — grief and wonder are allowed, but not indefinitely. The ascension comes with a promise of return, and an implicit nudge to get moving in the meantime.

chapters.title: With One Accord in Prayer
chapters.teaser: Before any public ministry begins, the earliest church is simply a room of people waiting together.
body: The upper room gathering (v.13-14) lists eleven apostles by name, alongside "the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brethren" — a broader group than the twelve alone, numbering about a hundred and twenty (v.15).

Their activity before Pentecost is deliberately unglamorous: continuing "with one accord in prayer and supplication." The church's public explosion in chapter 2 grows out of this quieter, communal waiting.

chapters.title: The Field of Blood
chapters.teaser: Peter recounts Judas's grim end as the assembled believers begin restoring their number.
body: Judas's death is described starkly — he "purchased a field with the reward of iniquity; and falling headlong, he burst asunder" (v.18) — and the field became known locally as Aceldama, "the field of blood" (v.19).

Peter treats even this grim detail as the fulfillment of scripture (v.16, 20), part of a broader instinct running through Acts: nothing that happens, however painful, falls outside of what God's larger story already anticipated.

chapters.title: The Lot Fell Upon Matthias
chapters.teaser: The remaining apostles fill Judas's vacant place using prayer and the casting of lots.
body: The qualification for the twelfth apostle is specific: someone who had been present "all the time that the Lord Jesus went in and out among us," from John's baptism through the ascension (v.21-22) — a firsthand witness, not simply an enthusiastic volunteer.

After narrowing the field to two candidates, the group prays and casts lots (v.24-26), an Old Testament method of discernment (compare Proverbs 16:33) that Acts uses here for the last time before Pentecost changes how guidance works.

chapters.title: Wind and Fire
chapters.teaser: The Spirit's arrival at Pentecost comes with dramatic, unmistakable physical signs.
body: "A sound from heaven as of a rushing mighty wind" fills the house, and something like "cloven tongues like as of fire" rests on each person present (v.2-3). Pentecost was already a Jewish harvest festival associated by tradition with the giving of the law at Sinai — so the Spirit's arrival on this exact day, with fire and a mighty sound, deliberately echoes Sinai's thunder and fire (Exodus 19).
Where Sinai gave a law written on stone, Pentecost gives a Spirit poured into people — the same divine drama, staged differently.

chapters.title: Every Man in His Own Tongue
chapters.teaser: A crowd of pilgrims from across the empire each hears the disciples speaking their native language.
body: The list of nations (v.9-11) — Parthians, Medes, Elamites, and more — reads almost like a roll call of the whole known world converging on Jerusalem for the feast, and each hears "the wonderful works of God" in their own birth tongue.

It reads as a pointed reversal of Babel in Genesis 11, where God confused human language to scatter a prideful, unified humanity. Here, instead of one language forced on everyone, many languages carry the same message — unity achieved without erasing difference.

chapters.title: This Is That Spoken by Joel
chapters.teaser: Peter's first sermon explains the strange scene by reaching back into the prophets.
body: Facing accusations of drunkenness, Peter's defense is essentially: it's only the third hour of the day (roughly 9am, v.15), and besides, this is exactly what the prophet Joel foretold — sons and daughters prophesying, young and old given visions and dreams (v.17-18).

Peter's sermon structure — quote scripture, then argue Jesus fulfills it — becomes the template for nearly every major speech in Acts that follows, from Stephen's in chapter 7 to Paul's in chapter 13.

chapters.title: What Shall We Do?
chapters.teaser: Peter's sermon lands hard, and the crowd's response is immediate and communal.
body: "They were pricked in their heart" (v.37) — a visceral, physical description of conviction — leads directly to a practical question, and Peter's answer is equally practical: repent, be baptized, receive the Spirit (v.38).

The scale of the response is staggering: about three thousand people are added "the same day" (v.41). The church that began as a hundred and twenty people praying in a room becomes, in a single afternoon, a movement.

chapters.title: All Things Common
chapters.teaser: The new believers respond to Pentecost by radically reshaping how they live together.
body: The chapter's closing description — devoted to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayer (v.42), selling possessions to meet each other's needs (v.44-45), eating together "with gladness and singleness of heart" (v.46) — reads less like a doctrine and more like a lived-out family.

The final line is almost casual in its power: "the Lord added to the church daily such as should be saved" (v.47). Growth, in this account, isn't engineered by a program — it follows naturally from a community that visibly shares everything, including its joy.

chapters.title: Silver and Gold Have I None
chapters.teaser: A lame beggar asks Peter and John for money, and gets something he wasn't expecting.
body: The man has been carried daily to the temple gate called Beautiful to beg — a routine so fixed that people recognize him instantly once he's healed (v.10). Peter's answer to his request for alms is blunt about what he lacks and confident about what he has: "such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk" (v.6).
It's a template for the kind of power the early church claims throughout Acts — not wealth or status, but authority borrowed entirely from Jesus's name.

chapters.title: Walking, and Leaping, and Praising God
chapters.teaser: The healed man's response is pure, uninhibited physical joy in the middle of the temple courts.
body: The healing is immediate and total — "his feet and ankle bones received strength" (v.7) — and his reaction matches the suddenness: he doesn't quietly walk away but leaps, walks, and enters the temple "walking, and leaping, and praising God" (v.8).
The public, physical nature of his joy is what draws the crowd that Peter then preaches to — the miracle itself becomes the occasion for the sermon, not a separate event from it.

chapters.title: Why Look Ye at Us?
chapters.teaser: Peter deflects credit for the miracle immediately, redirecting attention to Jesus.
body: As the astonished crowd gathers, Peter's first move is defensive against misplaced praise: "why look ye so earnestly on us, as though by our own power or holiness we had made this man to walk?" (v.12).

He then names the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob as the one who "hath glorified his Son Jesus" (v.13) — tying the miracle back to Israel's own ancestral story rather than presenting it as something new and disconnected from it.

chapters.title: Ye Denied the Holy One
chapters.teaser: Peter's sermon confronts his listeners directly with their role in Jesus's death, while offering them a way forward.
body: Peter doesn't soften the accusation — "ye denied the Holy One and the Just, and desired a murderer to be granted unto you" (v.14) — a direct reference to the crowd's earlier choice of Barabbas over Jesus.

But the accusation isn't the final word: "I wot that through ignorance ye did it" (v.17) opens a door to repentance rather than closing one, and the sermon pivots immediately into an invitation, not just an indictment.

chapters.title: Times of Refreshing
chapters.teaser: Peter closes his sermon with a vision of restoration that reaches back through Israel's prophets.
body: "Repent ye therefore, and be converted, that your sins may be blotted out, when the times of refreshing shall come" (v.19) frames repentance not just as guilt management but as participation in a larger, prophesied restoration.

Peter grounds the whole appeal in continuity, not novelty — Moses, Samuel, and "all the prophets" spoke of these days (v.22-24), and the promise to Abraham that "in thy seed shall all the kindreds of the earth be blessed" (v.25) is presented as being fulfilled right now, in this moment.

chapters.title: The Stone the Builders Rejected
chapters.teaser: Peter answers the council's interrogation by quoting a psalm about a rejected stone becoming the cornerstone.
body: Asked "by what power, or by what name" the healing happened (v.7), Peter — filled with the Holy Ghost — doesn't hedge. He quotes Psalm 118: Jesus is "the stone which was set at nought of you builders, which is become the head of the corner" (v.11), directly naming the council as the very builders who rejected him.
The claim that follows is total: "none other name under heaven given among men, whereby we must be saved" (v.12) — not one option among many religious paths, but the only one on offer.

chapters.title: Unlearned and Ignorant Men
chapters.teaser: The council is baffled by the boldness of two men without formal religious training.
body: The council's astonishment isn't really about the theology — it's about the speakers. Peter and John are recognizably "unlearned and ignorant men," lacking the rabbinic credentials that would normally command such confidence (v.13).

The explanation the council lands on is telling: "they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus." Association with Jesus, not formal training, is what the text credits for their boldness.

chapters.title: We Cannot But Speak
chapters.teaser: Ordered to stop preaching, Peter and John simply refuse, citing a higher obligation.
body: Commanded "not to speak at all nor teach in the name of Jesus" (v.18), the apostles' response is calm but immovable: "Whether it be right in the sight of God to hearken unto you more than unto God, judge ye" (v.19).

"We cannot but speak the things which we have seen and heard" (v.20) frames their disobedience not as defiance for its own sake, but as a simple incapacity to do otherwise — testimony they can't hold back.

chapters.title: Grant Unto Thy Servants Boldness
chapters.teaser: Released from custody, the believers respond to threats not with fear but with a prayer for courage.
body: Their prayer notably doesn't ask for safety or for the threats to stop — it asks God to "behold their threatenings" and then grant "boldness" to keep speaking, along with continued signs and wonders (v.29-30).

The answer is immediate and physical: "the place was shaken where they were assembled together; and they were all filled with the Holy Ghost" (v.31) — a visible, almost architectural confirmation that the prayer had been heard.

chapters.title: Of One Heart and One Soul
chapters.teaser: The believers' radical generosity is summarized, with Barnabas offered as a concrete example.
body: "Neither said any of them that ought of the things which he possessed was his own; but they had all things common" (v.32) describes an economic reality, not just a spiritual sentiment — property sold, proceeds distributed "according as he had need" (v.34-35).

Barnabas is introduced here almost as a case study — a Levite from Cyprus who sold land and laid the money at the apostles' feet (v.36-37) — someone whose generosity earns him a nickname that will define his role throughout the rest of Acts: "the son of consolation."

chapters.title: Why Hath Satan Filled Thine Heart?
chapters.teaser: Ananias and Sapphira sell property and secretly keep back part of the proceeds while claiming to give it all.
body: Unlike others who gave freely, Ananias and Sapphira sell a possession and quietly hold back part of the price while presenting the rest as the full amount (v.1-2). Peter's charge isn't that they kept money — that was entirely their right (v.4) — it's that they lied about it, and in doing so "lied... unto God" (v.4).
The sin the text names is deception dressed as devotion — performing generosity while withholding it, and getting caught not by human suspicion but by direct confrontation.

chapters.title: Great Fear Came Upon the Church
chapters.teaser: Both Ananias and Sapphira fall dead after being confronted, and the whole community is shaken.
body: The consequences are immediate and severe: Ananias falls dead upon hearing Peter's words (v.5), and three hours later, his wife — unaware of what happened — repeats the same lie and meets the same fate (v.7-10).

"Great fear came upon all the church, and upon as many as heard these things" (v.11) — the earliest community, capable of astonishing generosity, is shown here as capable of astonishing severity too, when its integrity is threatened from within.

chapters.title: The Shadow of Peter
chapters.teaser: Peter's healing ministry grows so renowned that people hope his mere shadow might help them.
body: Sick people are brought out into the streets on beds and couches, hoping that "at the least the shadow of Peter passing by might overshadow some of them" (v.15) — a striking, almost folk-religious expression of faith in the power working through him.

It's an image the text doesn't editorialize on, simply reports — a sign of how quickly and dramatically the apostles' reputation had spread beyond anything they likely anticipated back in the upper room.

chapters.title: The Angel Opened the Prison Doors
chapters.teaser: Jailed for their preaching, the apostles are freed overnight and go right back to teaching.
body: Imprisoned out of "indignation" from the Sadducees (v.17-18), the apostles are freed by an angel who opens the prison doors at night — and the instruction that follows is almost comically direct: "Go, stand and speak in the temple to the people all the words of this life" (v.20).

The council's confusion the next morning is understandable: the prison was "shut with all safety," guards still standing at the doors, yet "we found no man within" (v.23) — the apostles were back preaching exactly where they'd been arrested.

chapters.title: If It Be of God
chapters.teaser: A respected Pharisee talks the council out of executing the apostles with a simple test of time.
body: Gamaliel, a well-regarded teacher of the law, counsels patience rather than violence, citing two earlier failed movements — Theudas and Judas of Galilee — that collapsed once their leaders died (v.36-37).

His reasoning is pragmatic rather than theological: "if it be of men, it will come to nought: But if it be of God, ye cannot overthrow it" (v.38-39). The apostles are beaten and released, and leave "rejoicing that they were counted worthy to suffer shame for his name" (v.41) — treating punishment itself as a kind of honor.

chapters.title: Serve Tables
chapters.teaser: A practical dispute over food distribution forces the apostles to delegate responsibility for the first time.
body: Greek-speaking widows are being overlooked in the daily distribution of food, while Hebrew-speaking widows are not (v.1) — an early, very human tension inside a growing, ethnically mixed community. Rather than handle it personally, the twelve propose choosing seven others to manage it, freeing themselves for "prayer, and to the ministry of the word" (v.2-4).
It's the church's first structural decision, and it's driven by fairness for a marginalized group, not by administrative convenience alone.

chapters.title: Full of the Holy Ghost
chapters.teaser: The seven men chosen to serve tables all bear Greek names, quietly bridging the community's tension.
body: The qualifications set are spiritual as much as practical — "honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom" (v.3) — and notably, all seven names listed (Stephen, Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas) are Greek, suggesting the Hellenist minority whose widows were neglected is given real representation in the solution, not just a promise of better treatment.
The apostles then formally commission them with prayer and the laying on of hands (v.6) — the same gesture used elsewhere in Acts to mark someone as set apart for a task.

chapters.title: The Word of God Increased
chapters.teaser: A brief summary notes the church's remarkable growth, including converts from an unexpected direction.
body: "The word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly" (v.7) is a familiar refrain in Acts, but the detail that follows is surprising: "a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith" — conversion reaching into the very religious establishment that would soon oppose the church so fiercely.
It's a small, easy-to-miss line, but it complicates any simple picture of "the priests" as a uniform bloc of opposition.

chapters.title: None Able to Resist His Wisdom
chapters.teaser: Stephen's preaching draws fierce opposition precisely because no one can out-argue him.
body: Stephen, described as "full of faith and power," performs "great wonders and miracles" and draws debate from members of a synagogue representing several regions (v.8-9). The text is specific about why they turn to false witnesses instead of honest argument: "they were not able to resist the wisdom and the spirit by which he spake" (v.10).
Unable to win the argument, his opponents resort to fabricated testimony (v.11-13) — a pattern of persecution-by-slander that echoes how Jesus himself was tried.

chapters.title: The Face of an Angel
chapters.teaser: Facing a hostile council on false charges, Stephen's face is described in strikingly serene terms.
body: Set before the council on charges of blasphemy against the temple and the law, Stephen sits at the center of a hostile, staged accusation. Yet the observation the text offers is unexpected: "all that sat in the council... saw his face as it had been the face of an angel" (v.15).
It's a quiet, ominous close to the chapter — calm dignity in the face of a rigged trial, setting up the long speech and violent ending that follows in chapter 7.

chapters.title: The God of Glory Appeared
chapters.teaser: Stephen answers accusations about the temple by retelling Israel's story, starting far outside it.
body: Rather than directly defending himself, Stephen launches into a sweeping retelling of Israel's history, beginning with Abraham receiving a call from God while still in Mesopotamia, long before any temple or promised land existed (v.2-5).

The strategic point sits underneath the narrative choice: God has always worked with his people outside fixed geography and institutions, a claim that quietly undercuts the assumption that God's presence is tied to the Jerusalem temple.

chapters.title: Joseph, and God Was With Him
chapters.teaser: Stephen highlights a repeated biblical pattern: a rejected figure whom God vindicates anyway.
body: Stephen dwells on Joseph — sold by his own brothers out of envy, yet God was with him even in slavery and prison, eventually elevating him to save the very family that betrayed him (v.9-10).

The pattern is deliberate and building: God's chosen deliverers are repeatedly rejected by their own people before being vindicated. Stephen is laying groundwork, verse by verse, for a much sharper comparison still to come.

chapters.title: This Moses Whom They Refused
chapters.teaser: Stephen makes explicit what the Joseph story implied: Israel has a history of rejecting its own deliverers.
body: "This Moses whom they refused, saying, Who made thee a ruler and a judge? the same did God send to be a ruler and a deliverer" (v.35) states the pattern outright — the same generation that later celebrated Moses as its liberator had first rejected him.
By this point in the speech, the parallel to Jesus is unmistakable, even before Stephen says it directly: a deliverer sent by God, refused by his own people, later shown to have been right all along.

chapters.title: Dwelleth Not in Temples
chapters.teaser: Stephen finally addresses the temple charge directly, quoting Isaiah against an overly fixed view of God's presence.
body: Solomon built a house for God, Stephen concedes, but immediately qualifies it: "the most High dwelleth not in temples made with hands" (v.48), quoting Isaiah 66's image of heaven as God's throne and earth as his footstool — a God too large for any single building to contain.

It's the theological core of his defense: the charge against him assumed the temple was indispensable to God's presence, and Stephen argues, from scripture, that it never was in the way his accusers imagined.

chapters.title: Lord Jesus, Receive My Spirit
chapters.teaser: Stephen becomes the church's first martyr, dying in words that closely echo Jesus's own final moments.
body: Enraged by Stephen's closing accusation that they resist the Holy Ghost "as your fathers did" (v.51), the council drags him out and stones him. His final words — asking Jesus to receive his spirit and asking God not to hold the sin against his killers (v.59-60) — deliberately mirror Jesus's own words from the cross.

The chapter's last detail is easy to miss on a first read but crucial for what follows: "the witnesses laid down their clothes at a young man's feet, whose name was Saul" (v.58) — the first appearance of the man who will dominate the rest of the book.

chapters.title: Scattered, Preaching the Word
chapters.teaser: Persecution meant to crush the church instead spreads it far beyond Jerusalem.
body: Saul is "consenting unto" Stephen's death and begins actively hunting down believers, dragging them from their homes into prison (v.1-3). Yet the very persecution meant to destroy the movement scatters it into new territory — "they that were scattered abroad went every where preaching the word" (v.4).
It's an irony that becomes a pattern throughout Acts: opposition doesn't shut the mission down, it redistributes it, pushing the gospel exactly into the regions Jesus named back in chapter 1:8.

chapters.title: Simon the Sorcerer
chapters.teaser: A famous local magician believes and is baptized, but his old assumptions about power don't disappear.
body: Simon had "bewitched the people of Samaria" with sorcery and let them believe he was "some great one" (v.9-11) — until Philip's preaching and miracles draw the crowd's attention away, and Simon himself believes and is baptized (v.13).

His fascination with the apostles' "miracles and signs" suggests his conversion, while real, hasn't yet fully displaced the transactional way he understood spiritual power — a tension that surfaces immediately in what follows.

chapters.title: Thy Money Perish With Thee
chapters.teaser: Simon tries to buy the power to bestow the Holy Spirit, and Peter rebukes him sharply.
body: Watching the apostles lay hands on believers and impart the Holy Spirit, Simon offers money for the same ability (v.18-19) — treating a divine gift as a purchasable commodity, the same logic that had shaped his career as a sorcerer.

Peter's rebuke is severe: "Thy money perish with thee, because thou hast thought that the gift of God may be purchased with money" (v.20). The word "simony," for buying church office or spiritual power, comes directly from this episode.

chapters.title: Understandest Thou What Thou Readest?
chapters.teaser: Philip meets an Ethiopian official reading a prophecy he can't quite decipher, and offers to explain.
body: The Ethiopian eunuch — a high-ranking court official already reading Isaiah's prophecy about a suffering servant "led as a sheep to the slaughter" — admits he can't understand it "except some man should guide me" (v.30-31).

Philip, sent by the Spirit to join the chariot (v.29), "began at the same scripture, and preached unto him Jesus" (v.35) — treating that specific Isaiah passage as pointing directly to the crucifixion the eunuch had no framework yet to recognize.

chapters.title: See, Here Is Water
chapters.teaser: The eunuch asks a simple, direct question, and Philip baptizes him on the spot.
body: "See, here is water; what doth hinder me to be baptized?" (v.36) is remarkable partly for who's asking: a eunuch and a foreigner, two categories with restricted access under some readings of Old Testament law (Deuteronomy 23:1), now welcomed without hesitation.

The baptism happens immediately, and just as quickly Philip is "caught away" by the Spirit, leaving the eunuch to go "on his way rejoicing" (v.39) — the gospel's reach extending, in this single episode, to Africa and to someone outside the usual boundaries of full religious participation.

chapters.title: Why Persecutest Thou Me?
chapters.teaser: Saul, on his way to arrest believers, is confronted by a blinding light and a voice from heaven.
body: Saul is still "breathing out threatenings and slaughter" when a light from heaven stops him in his tracks near Damascus (v.1-3). The voice's question is pointed in an unexpected way: "Saul, Saul, why persecutest thou me?" (v.4) — Jesus identifies so closely with the church that attacking believers is attacking him directly.
Saul's own question in response — "Who art thou, Lord?" — shows he doesn't yet know who's speaking, even as he instinctively addresses him with a title of authority.

chapters.title: Scales Fell From His Eyes
chapters.teaser: Ananias overcomes real fear to obey a vision and restore Saul's sight.
body: Ananias's hesitation is entirely reasonable — he's heard "by many of this man, how much evil he hath done to thy saints at Jerusalem" (v.13) — yet he goes anyway, addressing his former persecutor with startling warmth: "Brother Saul" (v.17).

The physical detail is vivid: something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, and he immediately regains sight, is baptized, and eats for the first time in three days (v.18-19). Physical blindness and its healing frame the larger spiritual transformation taking place.

chapters.title: A Chosen Vessel
chapters.teaser: God tells Ananias that the church's fiercest enemy has just become one of its central figures.
body: God's description of Saul to Ananias reverses everything expected of him: "he is a chosen vessel unto me, to bear my name before the Gentiles, and kings, and the children of Israel" (v.15) — the persecutor is being repurposed as a missionary to the very range of peoples his mission will eventually reach.

The promise that follows is unusual for a commissioning: "I will shew him how great things he must suffer for my name's sake" (v.16) — not a promise of ease, but of purposeful suffering built into the calling from the very start.

chapters.title: Lowered Over the Wall
chapters.teaser: Saul's own former allies now want him dead, and he barely escapes the city.
body: The reversal is complete within just a few verses: Saul, who came to Damascus to arrest believers, now has to be smuggled out of the city by believers, lowered over the wall in a basket to escape a Jewish plot on his life (v.23-25).

Even in Jerusalem, the disciples are understandably wary of him at first — it takes Barnabas personally vouching for his conversion before the apostles accept him (v.26-27), a reminder of how much trust a changed reputation has to earn back.

chapters.title: Tabitha, Arise
chapters.teaser: Peter raises a beloved disciple from death in a scene that echoes Jesus's own miracles.
body: Tabitha (Dorcas), "full of good works and almsdeeds," dies at Joppa, and the grieving widows show Peter the clothes she'd made for them (v.36, 39) — a vivid, personal picture of exactly what her life had meant to the community.

Peter's raising of her — kneeling to pray, then commanding "Tabitha, arise" (v.40) — closely parallels Jesus's own raising of Jairus's daughter, and the result is the same kind of ripple effect: "many believed in the Lord" (v.42). The chapter ends with Peter staying in Joppa, setting the stage for the pivotal vision about to unfold there.

chapters.title: Cornelius, a Devout Man
chapters.teaser: A Roman centurion known for prayer and generosity receives a startling angelic visit.
body: Cornelius is introduced with unusual warmth for a Gentile occupier's officer: "a devout man, and one that feared God with all his house, which gave much alms to the people, and prayed to God alway" (v.2). His piety is genuine, even without formal membership in Israel's covenant community.
An angel tells him his prayers and alms have come up "for a memorial before God" (v.4) — language typically associated with acceptable temple offerings, applied here to a non-Jew's private devotion.

chapters.title: Rise, Peter; Kill and Eat
chapters.teaser: Peter sees a vision commanding him to eat animals his upbringing calls forbidden.
body: In a trance, Peter sees a sheet full of animals traditionally classified as unclean under Jewish law, and a voice tells him to kill and eat (v.11-13). His protest — "I have never eaten any thing that is common or unclean" — meets a pointed correction: "What God hath cleansed, that call not thou common" (v.14-15).

The vision repeats three times (v.16), and while Peter initially reads it only as being about food, its real target — arriving with Cornelius's messengers at that exact moment — turns out to be people, not diet.

chapters.title: God Is No Respecter of Persons
chapters.teaser: Standing in a Gentile home, Peter finally connects the vision's meaning to the people in front of him.
body: "Of a truth I perceive that God is no respecter of persons: But in every nation he that feareth him, and worketh righteousness, is accepted with him" (v.34-35) marks a genuine turning point in Peter's own understanding — not a truth he arrived preaching, but one the vision and the moment together revealed to him.
It's Peter thinking out loud in real time, connecting a dietary vision to a much larger theological shift about who belongs in God's household.

chapters.title: While Peter Yet Spake
chapters.teaser: The Holy Spirit falls on Cornelius's household before anyone has finished preaching or been baptized.
body: The Spirit's arrival interrupts Peter's own sermon — "While Peter yet spake these words, the Holy Ghost fell on all them which heard the word" (v.44) — a sequence that stuns the Jewish believers who came with him, astonished that Gentiles could receive the same gift "as well as we" (v.45-47).
The order matters: normally baptism preceded the Spirit's outpouring (as in ch.2 and ch.8), but here God acts first, leaving the human ritual to catch up to what's already happened.

chapters.title: Can Any Man Forbid Water?
chapters.teaser: Peter concludes there's no reasonable basis left to withhold baptism from the Gentiles present.
body: Having watched the Spirit fall on Cornelius's household exactly as it had on the disciples at Pentecost, Peter's question is almost rhetorical: "Can any man forbid water, that these should not be baptized, which have received the Holy Ghost as well as we?" (v.47).

The chapter that opened with a Roman officer's private prayers closes with his entire household formally welcomed into the church — a threshold moment the rest of Acts will spend considerable energy defending and working out in practice.

chapters.title: Thou Wentest In to Uncircumcised Men
chapters.teaser: Peter returns to Jerusalem and faces immediate pushback, not over doctrine but over table fellowship.
body: The Jerusalem believers' objection isn't primarily theological — it's social: "Thou wentest in to men uncircumcised, and didst eat with them" (v.3). Sharing meals with Gentiles violated deep-seated purity customs, regardless of any vision Peter might describe.
It's a reminder that even genuine spiritual breakthroughs still have to be worked out through very human, very practical friction — in this case, over who's allowed to sit at the same table.

chapters.title: Who Could Withstand God?
chapters.teaser: Peter defends his actions by simply retelling what happened, point by point, in order.
body: Peter doesn't argue theology in the abstract — he "rehearsed the matter from the beginning, and expounded it by order" (v.4), walking his critics through the vision, the messengers' arrival, and the Spirit falling on Cornelius's household exactly as it had at Pentecost (v.5-17).

His closing question disarms the objection entirely: "what was I, that I could withstand God?" (v.17). The argument that wins isn't clever rhetoric — it's an honest, sequential account of what God had already done.

chapters.title: Repentance Unto Life
chapters.teaser: The Jerusalem church, once persuaded, responds not with reluctant tolerance but with genuine praise.
body: "When they heard these things, they held their peace, and glorified God" (v.18) — the objection dissolves into worship once the full story is understood, a notable model for how conflict within the early church gets resolved throughout Acts: through patient explanation rather than authority alone.
"Then hath God also to the Gentiles granted repentance unto life" captures their conclusion precisely — not a grudging concession, but genuine recognition of what God had already decided.

chapters.title: Preaching the Lord Jesus to Grecians
chapters.teaser: Believers scattered by persecution start preaching to Gentiles in Antioch, and the church there takes off.
body: Some of those scattered after Stephen's death had been preaching only to Jews, but in Antioch, men from Cyprus and Cyrene start "speaking unto the Grecians, preaching the LORD Jesus" (v.19-20) — an organic, almost accidental expansion of the very inclusion Peter had just defended in Jerusalem.

Barnabas, sent to investigate, doesn't come to police the movement but to encourage it, and then goes to find Saul specifically to help teach the growing community (v.22-25) — a partnership that will shape the rest of the book.

chapters.title: Called Christians First in Antioch
chapters.teaser: A new name for the movement emerges in Antioch, alongside a practical act of cross-cultural generosity.
body: The detail that "the disciples were called Christians first in Antioch" (v.26) marks a turning point — the movement is visibly becoming something distinct, no longer easily folded into existing categories.

When a prophet named Agabus predicts a coming famine, the Antioch believers respond concretely, sending relief "to the brethren which dwelt in Judaea" (v.27-30) — a Gentile-heavy church materially supporting its Jewish counterpart, living out in practice the unity Peter had just defended in principle.

chapters.title: He Killed James With the Sword
chapters.teaser: Herod's persecution claims an apostle's life in a single, unadorned sentence.
body: The report of James's death is strikingly brief and matter-of-fact — "he killed James the brother of John with the sword" (v.2) — no elaboration, no drama, just a flat statement of the first apostolic martyrdom, distinct in tone from the far more detailed account of Stephen's death in chapter 7.
Herod, sensing the execution "pleased the Jews," moves immediately to arrest Peter as well (v.3), suggesting political calculation rather than deep conviction was driving the persecution.

chapters.title: Prayer Made Without Ceasing
chapters.teaser: As Peter sits in prison awaiting execution, the church's only recorded response is sustained prayer.
body: With Peter imprisoned under heavy guard — four squads of soldiers, chained between two of them (v.4, 6) — the church's response is described simply: "prayer was made without ceasing of the church unto God for him" (v.5).
It's a deliberate contrast: overwhelming military security on one side, persistent unarmed prayer on the other, and the chapter is about to show which one actually determines the outcome.

chapters.title: Sleeping Between Two Soldiers
chapters.teaser: An angel rescues Peter from prison so gently that he initially thinks he's dreaming.
body: Peter is found asleep the night before his expected execution — remarkably calm given the circumstances — when an angel strikes him awake, and his chains simply fall off (v.6-7). Even walking past two guard posts and through a gate that opens by itself, Peter "wist not that it was true... but thought he saw a vision" (v.9).
The escape is deliberately understated and almost dreamlike, only becoming real to Peter once he's alone in the street and "come to himself" (v.11).

chapters.title: It Is His Angel
chapters.teaser: The praying church doesn't believe its own prayer has been answered when Peter shows up at the door.
body: Rhoda, a servant girl, is so overjoyed at recognizing Peter's voice that she runs to tell everyone without actually opening the gate (v.13-14) — and the praying believers inside dismiss her, insisting "it is his angel" rather than believing Peter himself could be free (v.15).
It's a gently comic, very human detail: a church that has been praying fervently for Peter's release still can't quite believe it when the answer is standing at the door.

chapters.title: Eaten of Worms
chapters.teaser: Herod's fatal end for accepting worship as a god is set directly against the gospel's unstoppable growth.
body: Herod, dressed in royal apparel and addressed by the crowd as a god's voice rather than a man's, accepts the flattery without objection — and "immediately the angel of the Lord smote him, because he gave not God the glory" (v.21-23), a gruesome death by illness described as being "eaten of worms."

The chapter's closing line lands with quiet emphasis after that grim detail: "But the word of God grew and multiplied" (v.24). Political power proves fragile and temporary; the message it tried to suppress keeps expanding regardless.

chapters.title: Separate Me Barnabas and Saul
chapters.teaser: The Antioch church commissions its first missionary journey at the Holy Spirit's direct instruction.
body: During a time of worship and fasting, the Spirit speaks with unusual directness: "Separate me Barnabas and Saul for the work whereunto I have called them" (v.2) — the initiative for what becomes Paul's first missionary journey comes not from a strategic plan but from the leading of the Spirit within ordinary worship.
The response is simple and formal: fasting, prayer, laying on of hands, and sending them off (v.3) — a template of commissioning that will recur throughout the missionary movement Acts describes.

chapters.title: Child of the Devil
chapters.teaser: Paul confronts a sorcerer trying to block a Roman official from hearing the gospel — and the sorcerer goes blind.
body: Elymas the sorcerer actively works to "turn away the deputy from the faith" (v.8), and Paul's rebuke is severe: "O full of all subtilty and all mischief, thou child of the devil... wilt thou not cease to pervert the right ways of the Lord?" (v.10).

The resulting blindness — "not seeing the sun for a season" (v.11) — pointedly recalls Paul's own temporary blindness after his conversion in chapter 9, a judgment that echoes the very mercy once shown to him.

chapters.title: Saul, Who Also Is Called Paul
chapters.teaser: The narrative quietly shifts from calling him "Saul" to "Paul" right as his mission turns toward the Gentile world.
body: Verse 9 marks the transition almost in passing — "Then Saul, (who also is called Paul)" — and from this point forward, Acts consistently uses the Roman name Paul rather than the Hebrew name Saul.

The timing isn't incidental: the shift happens exactly as the mission moves further into Gentile, Roman-influenced territory, subtly matching the missionary's public name to the audience he's now increasingly addressing.

chapters.title: A Man After Mine Own Heart
chapters.teaser: Paul's synagogue sermon retraces Israel's history, much like Stephen's speech, but ends with the resurrection.
body: Paul's sermon in Pisidian Antioch follows a familiar shape — reviewing Israel's history from Egypt through the judges to David (v.17-22) — but pivots to declare Jesus the promised "Saviour" from David's own line (v.23), someone whom "God raised... from the dead" after his rulers failed to recognize him (v.30).

Where Stephen's speech in chapter 7 built toward an accusation, Paul's builds toward an offer — "through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins" (v.38) — the same historical pattern used for a different rhetorical purpose.

chapters.title: We Turn to the Gentiles
chapters.teaser: Rejected by the Jewish leaders in the synagogue, Paul and Barnabas make a pivotal, programmatic decision.
body: Facing envy and contradiction from the Jewish leaders after the following week's crowd swells with Gentile interest (v.44-45), Paul and Barnabas respond with a declaration that will recur throughout Acts: "lo, we turn to the Gentiles" (v.46), grounded in Isaiah's prophecy of a "light of the Gentiles... unto the ends of the earth" (v.47).

Expelled from the region, they shake the dust off their feet — a symbolic act of finality — and leave "filled with joy, and with the Holy Ghost" (v.51-52), a striking emotional response to what looks, on the surface, like defeat.

chapters.title: A Great Multitude Believed
chapters.teaser: In Iconium, both Jews and Greeks respond to the gospel, while opposition builds at the same time.
body: "A great multitude both of the Jews and also of the Greeks believed" (v.1), while unbelieving Jews simultaneously stir up hostility among the Gentiles — a pattern of mixed, divided response that recurs across nearly every city Paul visits.

The apostles stay anyway, "speaking boldly in the Lord," and their persistence is met with confirming signs and wonders even as "the multitude of the city was divided" (v.3-4) — belief and opposition growing side by side, not one replacing the other.

chapters.title: The Gods Are Come Down
chapters.teaser: A healing in Lystra convinces the crowd that Paul and Barnabas are pagan gods in disguise.
body: After healing a man crippled from birth, the crowd doesn't credit the God of Israel — they reach for their own mythology, declaring "The gods are come down to us in the likeness of men," naming Barnabas as Zeus and Paul, the more talkative one, as Hermes (v.11-12).

The misunderstanding is so complete that the local priest of Zeus arrives with oxen, ready to offer sacrifice to them (v.13) — a vivid picture of how easily genuine divine power can be reinterpreted through an entirely different religious framework.

chapters.title: Men of Like Passions With You
chapters.teaser: Paul and Barnabas are horrified by the worship and insist, urgently, that they're ordinary men.
body: Their reaction to being worshiped is visceral — they tear their own clothes and run into the crowd protesting, "We also are men of like passions with you" (v.14-15) — refusing a status that would have been easy to simply accept.

Instead of taking the credit, they redirect the crowd toward "the living God, which made heaven, and earth, and the sea," pointing to rain and harvest as evidence of a generous creator who "left not himself without witness" even among people who'd never heard of Israel's scriptures (v.15-17).

chapters.title: Stoned and Left for Dead
chapters.teaser: The same crowd that wanted to worship Paul turns violently against him within the same chapter.
body: Jews arriving from Antioch and Iconium persuade the crowd to turn against Paul entirely, stoning him and dragging him out of the city, "supposing he had been dead" (v.19) — a jarring reversal from a people who, just verses earlier, wanted to offer him sacrifices.

Paul's recovery is described with startling brevity: he simply "rose up, and came into the city" and left for Derbe the next day (v.20) — resilience stated almost without comment, letting the action speak for itself.

chapters.title: Confirming the Souls of the Disciples
chapters.teaser: Paul and Barnabas retrace their route, strengthening the very churches born out of persecution and confusion.
body: Rather than pressing further outward, they deliberately return through the cities where they'd just been stoned, mistaken for gods, and divided the crowds — appointing elders in each church and preparing new believers for what's ahead: "we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God" (v.21-23).

Reporting back to Antioch, they emphasize not their own achievement but "how he had opened the door of faith unto the Gentiles" (v.27) — closing the loop on a journey that began with a Spirit-led commissioning back in chapter 13.

chapters.title: Except Ye Be Circumcised
chapters.teaser: A controversy over circumcision threatens to derail the entire Gentile mission.
body: Certain men from Judea teach that Gentile believers "cannot be saved" without circumcision according to the law of Moses (v.1) — a direct challenge to everything Paul and Barnabas have just spent a chapter building among Gentile converts.

The dispute is serious enough that the Antioch church sends Paul and Barnabas to Jerusalem to settle it with the apostles and elders (v.2) — the first major theological council in the church's history, convened because the stakes for the mission's future were too high to leave unresolved.

chapters.title: No Difference Between Us
chapters.teaser: Peter reminds the council that God already settled this question at Cornelius's house.
body: Peter's speech leans on his own earlier experience rather than abstract argument: God "put no difference between us and them, purifying their hearts by faith" when the Spirit fell on Cornelius's household (v.8-9) — the events of chapter 10 becoming the decisive precedent here.

His closing question is pointed: why "tempt God, to put a yoke upon the neck of the disciples, which neither our fathers nor we were able to bear" (v.10) — arguing that even Israel itself hadn't managed to fully keep the law, so it shouldn't be imposed as a barrier to Gentile inclusion now.

chapters.title: James Answered
chapters.teaser: James, leading the Jerusalem church, settles the debate by appealing to prophecy about Gentile inclusion.
body: James quotes the prophet Amos on God rebuilding "the tabernacle of David... that the residue of men might seek after the Lord, and all the Gentiles" (v.16-17) — framing Gentile inclusion not as a new development but as something the prophets had already anticipated.

His judgment carries real authority in the room: "we trouble not them, which from among the Gentiles are turned to God" (v.19) — resolving the debate in favor of the Gentile mission while still proposing a few practical guidelines to ease shared life between Jewish and Gentile believers.

chapters.title: Seemed Good to the Spirit
chapters.teaser: The council's decree keeps only a handful of requirements, easing table fellowship between Jewish and Gentile believers.
body: The final letter asks Gentile believers to abstain from just four things — food offered to idols, blood, meat from strangled animals, and sexual immorality (v.20, 29) — a minimal list compared to the full weight of Mosaic law, aimed at practical matters that would otherwise make shared meals between Jewish and Gentile believers impossible.

The phrase "it seemed good to the Holy Ghost, and to us" (v.28) is a striking claim of collaborative discernment — the council presents its decision as genuinely joint work between divine guidance and human deliberation, not one substituting for the other.

chapters.title: The Contention Was So Sharp
chapters.teaser: Right after a triumphant council, Paul and Barnabas split over a personal disagreement about John Mark.
body: Barnabas wants to bring John Mark on the next journey; Paul refuses, since Mark had abandoned them partway through the previous trip (v.37-38). The disagreement escalates into "contention... so sharp, that they departed asunder one from the other" (v.39).

It's an unusually honest note to include right after the council's unity — a reminder that theological agreement doesn't guarantee personal harmony, even between two men who had ministered side by side for years. The story doesn't hide the fracture; it simply lets both men go their separate ways, each still doing the work.

chapters.title: Timotheus, Circumcised for the Jews' Sake
chapters.teaser: Paul circumcises Timothy despite the Jerusalem council's ruling, for the sake of practical mission strategy.
body: Timothy, whose mother was Jewish and father Greek, is circumcised by Paul "because of the Jews which were in those quarters" (v.3) — a striking choice given that the council in chapter 15 had just ruled circumcision unnecessary for Gentile believers.

The decision reads as pragmatic rather than theological: Paul isn't reversing the council's ruling, he's removing an unnecessary obstacle to Timothy's credibility with Jewish audiences he'll need to reach.

chapters.title: Come Over Into Macedonia
chapters.teaser: A nighttime vision redirects the mission's geography, and the narrator quietly joins the journey.
body: Forbidden by the Spirit from preaching in Asia and blocked again from entering Bithynia (v.6-7), Paul receives a vision of a Macedonian man pleading, "Come over into Macedonia, and help us" (v.9) — the missionary team reading this as God's clear redirection.

Verse 10 marks a subtle but significant shift in the text itself: "we endeavoured to go into Macedonia" — the narration switches to first person, suggesting Luke, the traditional author of Acts, has now joined the traveling group in person.

chapters.title: Lydia, a Seller of Purple
chapters.teaser: The gospel's first recorded European convert is a successful businesswoman who opens her home.
body: Lydia, a dealer in expensive purple dye and cloth, listens to Paul at a riverside prayer gathering, and "the Lord opened" her heart to respond (v.14). Her household is baptized, and she insists Paul's team stay in her home (v.15).

It's a notable detail that the first named convert in what becomes European Christianity is an independent, financially capable woman, and that her hospitality becomes the group's first foothold in the region.

chapters.title: At Midnight They Sang Praises
chapters.teaser: Beaten and imprisoned unjustly, Paul and Silas respond by singing, and an earthquake follows.
body: After casting a spirit of divination out of an enslaved girl — disrupting the profit her owners made from her fortune-telling — Paul and Silas are beaten and thrown into the inner prison, feet fastened in stocks (v.16-24).

Their response at midnight is remarkable: praying and singing hymns, with "the prisoners" listening (v.25). The earthquake that follows frees everyone's chains, yet Paul stops the jailer from suicide and stays put, turning the crisis into the jailer's own conversion (v.26-33).

chapters.title: Being Romans
chapters.teaser: Paul reveals his Roman citizenship only after the illegal punishment, using it to demand accountability.
body: Having been beaten and jailed without trial, Paul waits until the magistrates try to quietly release them before objecting: "They have beaten us openly uncondemned, being Romans... let them come themselves and fetch us out" (v.37).

The magistrates are visibly afraid once they learn the truth (v.38) — a reminder that Paul's citizenship functions throughout Acts as a real, strategic legal tool, used deliberately and at specific moments rather than as a shield he leans on constantly.

chapters.title: Turned the World Upside Down
chapters.teaser: Paul's opponents in Thessalonica describe the gospel's disruptive power in their own hostile words.
body: Unable to find Paul and Silas, a mob drags other believers before the city rulers, shouting an accusation that inadvertently captures the movement's real impact: "These that have turned the world upside down are come hither also" (v.6).

It's a phrase meant as condemnation that reads, from the outside, almost like a compliment — even the gospel's fiercest opponents recognized how thoroughly it was reordering people's lives and loyalties.

chapters.title: More Noble Than Those in Thessalonica
chapters.teaser: The Bereans are praised specifically for testing Paul's teaching against scripture rather than just accepting it.
body: The Bereans "received the word with all readiness of mind, and searched the scriptures daily, whether those things were so" (v.11) — a combination of openness and scrutiny that Acts singles out for special praise.
It's a notable model: eager reception isn't presented as opposed to careful verification. The text commends both together, treating credulity and skepticism alike as incomplete without the other.

chapters.title: Wholly Given to Idolatry
chapters.teaser: Paul's reaction to Athens's abundance of idols becomes the occasion for his most philosophically engaged sermon.
body: Waiting in Athens, Paul's "spirit was stirred in him, when he saw the city wholly given to idolatry" (v.16) — a visceral, personal reaction that leads him into daily debate in the marketplace with whoever happens to be there, including Epicurean and Stoic philosophers (v.17-18).

Some dismiss him as a "babbler," a term for someone who scavenges bits of ideas without real understanding — an insult that, ironically, sets up one of the most intellectually serious speeches in the entire New Testament.

chapters.title: To the Unknown God
chapters.teaser: Paul builds his most sophisticated argument around an altar Athenians built to a god they couldn't name.
body: Rather than opening with scripture, Paul starts from something his Athenian audience already had: an altar inscribed "TO THE UNKNOWN GOD" (v.23) — using their own religious anxiety about missing a deity as the entry point for introducing the true one.

He even quotes their own poets — "we are also his offspring" (v.28) — building common ground methodically before turning to the resurrection, the one claim his philosophically sophisticated audience finds hardest to accept (v.31-32).

chapters.title: Some Mocked, Others Believed
chapters.teaser: The Areopagus speech ends with a genuinely mixed verdict, not a clean triumph or a clean failure.
body: The resurrection claim splits the room exactly along the lines you'd expect from Greek philosophy, which generally saw the body as something to escape, not something worth restoring: some mock outright, others politely defer ("We will hear thee again of this matter," v.32), and only a few actually believe, including Dionysius the Areopagite and a woman named Damaris (v.34).
It's an honest, unglamorous ending for what is often remembered as Paul's greatest sermon — real intellectual engagement, and still, only a modest handful of converts to show for it.

chapters.title: Aquila and Priscilla, Tentmakers
chapters.teaser: Paul supports himself with ordinary manual labor while building the church in Corinth.
body: Paul finds work and lodging with Aquila and Priscilla, a Jewish couple recently expelled from Rome, "because he was of the same craft" — tentmaking (v.2-3). Ministry and manual labor sit side by side without tension in this account, Paul reasoning in the synagogue on the sabbath and working the rest of the week.
The partnership with this couple becomes significant well beyond shared trade — they travel with Paul afterward and later play a key role in mentoring another major figure, Apollos.

chapters.title: Much People in This City
chapters.teaser: A night vision reassures Paul of safety and results just as opposition intensifies.
body: Facing hostility after the Jews "opposed themselves, and blasphemed" his message (v.6), Paul receives a vision at night: "Be not afraid, but speak, and hold not thy peace: For I am with thee... I have much people in this city" (v.9-10).

The promise of unseen future converts — people not yet identified as believers — becomes the basis for an unusually long stay: eighteen months teaching in Corinth (v.11), longer than almost any other single stop in Paul's travels recorded in Acts.

chapters.title: Gallio Cared for None
chapters.teaser: A Roman official's indifference to a religious dispute inadvertently protects the church's legal standing.
body: When Jewish leaders bring Paul before the Roman proconsul Gallio, hoping for a conviction, Gallio refuses to even hear the case, dismissing it as an internal Jewish argument over "words and names, and of your law" rather than a matter of Roman criminal justice (v.14-15).

His indifference — he "cared for none of those things" even when the crowd beats the synagogue ruler in front of him (v.17) — sets an informal but useful precedent: Roman authority, at least in this instance, declines to treat the gospel's spread as a punishable civil offense.

chapters.title: Having a Vow
chapters.teaser: A small personal detail shows Paul continuing distinctly Jewish religious practices even deep into his Gentile mission.
body: Before sailing from Cenchrea, Paul has his head shaved, "for he had a vow" (v.18) — likely a Nazirite-style vow described in Numbers 6, a marker of devoted Jewish piety that sits easily alongside his role as apostle to the Gentiles.

It's a quiet reminder that Paul's theology of Gentile inclusion never meant abandoning his own Jewish identity and practice — the two are held together without apparent contradiction throughout his ministry.

chapters.title: Knowing Only the Baptism of John
chapters.teaser: A gifted, eloquent preacher is quietly corrected in private by two believers he'd never have expected to teach him.
body: Apollos is described in glowing terms — eloquent, "mighty in the scriptures," fervent in spirit — yet his knowledge has a real gap: he knows "only the baptism of John" (v.24-25), an earlier, incomplete stage of the message.

Aquila and Priscilla don't correct him publicly or dismiss his gifting; they take him aside and "expounded unto him the way of God more perfectly" (v.26) — a quiet, humble model of correction that strengthens rather than sidelines a genuinely talented teacher.

chapters.title: Have Ye Received the Holy Ghost?
chapters.teaser: Paul finds disciples in Ephesus who don't even know the Holy Spirit has been given.
body: The disciples Paul meets in Ephesus answer his question about the Holy Spirit with genuine confusion: "We have not so much as heard whether there be any Holy Ghost" (v.2). Their baptism, it turns out, was only John's baptism of repentance — pointing forward to someone still to come (v.3-4).

Once Paul explains and baptizes them properly, the Spirit comes with visible signs — tongues and prophecy (v.6) — closing a gap in their understanding that had left them, until that point, only partway into the story.

chapters.title: Handkerchiefs and Aprons
chapters.teaser: God works unusually tangible miracles through objects that had merely touched Paul's body.
body: "From his body were brought unto the sick handkerchiefs or aprons, and the diseases departed from them, and the evil spirits went out of them" (v.12) — an unusually physical, almost superstitious-sounding form of healing that the text simply reports without extensive comment.

It recalls other moments in the New Testament where touch and proximity carry healing power (the woman with the issue of blood, Peter's shadow in chapter 5) — a recurring motif of God working through ordinary physical contact, not only direct spiritual encounter.

chapters.title: I Know Jesus and Paul
chapters.teaser: Seven brothers try to use Jesus's name like a magic formula, and it backfires violently.
body: The sons of Sceva attempt to exorcise a demon by invoking "Jesus whom Paul preacheth" (v.13) as if it were a formula rather than a relationship — and the possessed man turns on them, beating them so badly they flee "naked and wounded" (v.16).

The demon's own reply is the sharpest part of the episode: "Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are ye?" (v.15) — a pointed distinction between authority borrowed from genuine relationship and authority merely imitated.

chapters.title: They Burned Their Books
chapters.teaser: Ephesian converts publicly destroy their occult texts at enormous personal cost.
body: Fear spreads through the city after the sons of Sceva incident, and many who had practiced "curious arts" — magic — bring their books together and burn them publicly, books valued at fifty thousand pieces of silver (v.18-19), an enormous sum representing years of income.

The public, costly, and voluntary nature of the burning marks it as more than mere embarrassment — it's presented as decisive repentance, a visible break with an entire former way of life rather than a private change of belief.

chapters.title: Great Is Diana of the Ephesians
chapters.teaser: A riot erupts not primarily over theology but over threatened profits from idol-making.
body: Demetrius the silversmith openly states his real concern: Paul's preaching is convincing people that handmade gods aren't gods at all, threatening "this our craft" and the livelihood built around producing shrines for the goddess Diana (v.24-27).

The resulting riot — two hours of chanting in a packed theater (v.34) — is defused not by theological argument but by a practical civic official warning the crowd about the legal risk of an unauthorized public disturbance (v.35-41). It's a clear-eyed reminder that opposition to the gospel in Acts is often driven as much by threatened money and status as by genuine religious conviction.

chapters.title: Fell Down From the Third Loft
chapters.teaser: A young man dies falling asleep during Paul's overlong sermon, and is raised back to life.
body: Eutychus, sitting in a window during Paul's late-night preaching, drifts off and falls from the third story, "taken up dead" (v.9) — an almost darkly comic detail about just how long Paul's farewell sermon ran.

Paul's response is calm and immediate: he falls on the young man, embraces him, and declares "his life is in him" (v.10) — then simply continues talking with the gathered believers until daybreak, the miracle folded into the evening's events rather than treated as its climax.

chapters.title: I Kept Back Nothing
chapters.teaser: Paul summarizes his ministry ethic to the Ephesian elders as one of total transparency.
body: Meeting the Ephesian elders at Miletus, Paul reviews his time among them: serving "with all humility of mind, and with many tears," teaching "publickly, and from house to house," holding nothing back that would be profitable to them (v.18-20).

It reads as both a personal testimony and an implicit standard he's setting for the leaders he's about to leave behind — transparency and full disclosure as the baseline expectation for anyone shepherding a congregation.

chapters.title: Bonds and Afflictions Abide Me
chapters.teaser: Paul heads toward Jerusalem knowing, through repeated prophetic warning, that suffering awaits him there.
body: "The Holy Ghost witnesseth in every city, saying that bonds and afflictions abide me" (v.23) — Paul isn't walking into danger unknowingly; he's been repeatedly warned and goes anyway, prioritizing "finish my course with joy" over self-preservation (v.24).
It's a striking picture of resolve grounded not in ignorance of the risk but in full, repeated awareness of it — courage that has already counted the cost before taking the next step.

chapters.title: Grievous Wolves Shall Enter In
chapters.teaser: Paul warns the elders that the greatest threat to the church will come from within its own leadership.
body: "After my departing shall grievous wolves enter in among you, not sparing the flock. Also of your own selves shall men arise, speaking perverse things" (v.29-30) — a sobering warning that danger to the church won't only come from outside persecution, but from corrupted leadership within.

The charge that follows — "feed the church of God, which he hath purchased with his own blood" (v.28) — grounds pastoral responsibility in the highest possible stakes: the church belongs to God at the cost of Christ's own life, and its leaders are answerable for how they treat it.

chapters.title: More Blessed to Give
chapters.teaser: Paul closes his farewell with a saying of Jesus preserved nowhere else in the New Testament.
body: "Remember the words of the Lord Jesus, how he said, It is more blessed to give than to receive" (v.35) is one of the very few sayings of Jesus recorded in the New Testament outside the four Gospels — preserved here only because Paul happened to pass it along.

The farewell scene that follows is openly emotional — weeping, embracing, kissing (v.37) — grief made sharper by Paul's own statement that "they should see his face no more." It's one of the most tender, unguarded moments in the entire book.

chapters.title: They Kneeled Down on the Shore
chapters.teaser: A departing congregation walks Paul's group all the way to the beach for a final prayer together.
body: At Tyre, the whole community — including wives and children — accompanies Paul's group "till we were out of the city," kneeling together on the shore to pray before the ship departs (v.5-6).

It's a small, tender detail of communal devotion: an entire congregation, not just its leaders, taking the time to see Paul off properly, treating the departure as something worth a shared, deliberate goodbye.

chapters.title: Four Daughters Which Did Prophesy
chapters.teaser: Philip's household includes four unmarried daughters recognized for a prophetic gift.
body: Staying with Philip the evangelist in Caesarea, the text notes almost in passing that he "had four daughters, virgins, which did prophesy" (v.9) — a brief but notable detail about women exercising a recognized spiritual gift within the early church.

The Gospel's promise from Acts 2 — that God would pour out his Spirit so that "your daughters shall prophesy" — finds a quiet, concrete fulfillment in this one household, stated without any special comment or controversy.

chapters.title: Agabus Bound His Own Hands
chapters.teaser: A prophet dramatizes his warning to Paul by literally binding himself with Paul's own belt.
body: Agabus doesn't just predict Paul's coming arrest — he acts it out, taking Paul's girdle and binding his own hands and feet, declaring, "So shall the Jews at Jerusalem bind the man that owneth this girdle" (v.11), a dramatic prophetic sign-act echoing similar visual prophecies from Isaiah, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel.
The vivid, physical nature of the warning makes the coming danger impossible to dismiss as vague or abstract — everyone present understands exactly what's being predicted.

chapters.title: The Will of the Lord
chapters.teaser: Paul's friends beg him not to go to Jerusalem, and ultimately yield to his resolve.
body: Paul's response to the warnings and pleading is emotionally direct: "What mean ye to weep and to break mine heart? for I am ready not to be bound only, but also to die at Jerusalem" (v.13).

His companions, unable to change his mind, land on acceptance rather than continued resistance: "The will of the Lord be done" (v.14) — a submission that doesn't require agreeing with the decision, only trusting the one making it.

chapters.title: All the City Was Moved
chapters.teaser: A false accusation in the temple triggers a riot and Paul's arrest, launching the book's final section.
body: Jews from Asia falsely accuse Paul of bringing a Gentile into a restricted area of the temple (v.28-29), and the resulting uproar is citywide: "all the city was moved, and the people ran together" (v.30), the crowd beating Paul until Roman soldiers intervene and take him into custody.

This arrest opens the long final movement of Acts — trials, hearings, and appeals that will occupy the rest of the book, moving Paul steadily, through legal machinery rather than free travel, toward Rome.

chapters.title: He Spake in the Hebrew Tongue
chapters.teaser: Paul quiets a hostile crowd simply by addressing them in their own sacred language.
body: Facing an angry mob just after his arrest, Paul asks permission to speak, and "when they heard that he spake in the Hebrew tongue to them, they kept the more silence" (v.2) — a rhetorical move that buys him a genuine hearing before he's said a single substantive word.
It's a small but telling detail about Paul's approach throughout Acts: he consistently meets audiences on their own linguistic and cultural terms before challenging their assumptions.

chapters.title: At the Feet of Gamaliel
chapters.teaser: Paul establishes his credentials as a zealous, trained Jew before saying anything about Jesus.
body: Paul lays out his background carefully: born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem, trained under the respected teacher Gamaliel (the same Gamaliel who counseled patience toward the apostles back in chapter 5), "zealous toward God, as ye all are this day" (v.3).
It's a deliberate rhetorical strategy — establishing deep common ground and shared zeal with his accusers before pivoting to the experience that changed everything for him.

chapters.title: Why Persecutest Thou Me?
chapters.teaser: Paul retells his conversion story for the crowd, in his own voice, for the first time in Acts.
body: Though the reader has already encountered Saul's conversion narrated by Luke in chapter 9, this is the first time Paul tells it himself, in the first person, to a hostile audience — the same core details (the light, the voice, the blindness, Ananias) now offered as personal testimony rather than third-person narration.
Acts will repeat this story a third time in chapter 26, a level of repetition that signals just how central this single event is to the whole book's understanding of Paul's calling.

chapters.title: Sent to the Gentiles
chapters.teaser: One specific word in Paul's testimony reignites the crowd's fury and ends his hearing.
body: The crowd listens patiently through most of Paul's account, right up until he quotes God's commissioning: "Depart: for I will send thee far hence unto the Gentiles" (v.21). That single word — Gentiles — is what finally breaks their willingness to listen.

"They gave him audience unto this word" (v.22), and then erupt, demanding his death — a stark illustration of exactly how threatening the idea of full Gentile inclusion remained to many within Judaism at the time.

chapters.title: Lawful to Scourge a Roman?
chapters.teaser: Paul invokes his citizenship just before an illegal punishment begins, stopping it immediately.
body: As soldiers prepare to interrogate Paul "by scourging" without trial, he asks the centurion a pointed legal question: "Is it lawful for you to scourge a man that is a Roman, and uncondemned?" (v.25).

The effect is immediate — the chief captain himself grows "afraid" once he realizes he'd bound a Roman citizen without due process (v.29). Roman law, elsewhere used to persecute Paul, here functions as unexpected protection.

chapters.title: Thou Whited Wall
chapters.teaser: Paul lashes out at the high priest, then walks back his words once he learns who he'd insulted.
body: Struck on the order of the high priest Ananias, Paul responds sharply: "God shall smite thee, thou whited wall" (v.3) — a vivid insult picturing a wall painted to look clean while rotting underneath.

When told he's just insulted God's high priest, Paul immediately backs down, citing scripture against speaking evil of a ruler (v.5) — an honest, unflattering moment where even Paul's own temper gets the better of him before he corrects course.

chapters.title: Of the Hope of the Resurrection
chapters.teaser: Paul splits a hostile council by identifying a doctrinal fault line running straight through it.
body: Recognizing the council is divided between Sadducees, who deny any resurrection, and Pharisees, who affirm it, Paul declares himself "a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee" being questioned specifically over "the hope and resurrection of the dead" (v.6).

The tactic works immediately — the council fractures into an internal argument so fierce that Roman soldiers have to physically remove Paul before he's "pulled in pieces" (v.10), a strategic move that turns a unified threat into a divided, ineffective one.

chapters.title: Be of Good Cheer, at Rome
chapters.teaser: The Lord appears to Paul at night, connecting his present danger to a specific future destination.
body: "The night following the Lord stood by him, and said, Be of good cheer, Paul: for as thou hast testified of me in Jerusalem, so must thou bear witness also at Rome" (v.11) — a promise that ties this dark moment directly to the goal Paul had already named for himself back in chapter 19.
It's a pattern that recurs at Paul's lowest points throughout the second half of Acts: not rescue from danger, but reassurance of ultimate purpose within it.

chapters.title: More Than Forty Conspirators
chapters.teaser: A group of men vow to fast until they've killed Paul, and the plot nearly succeeds.
body: More than forty men bind themselves under an oath "that they will neither eat nor drink till they have killed Paul" (v.12-14) — a serious, coordinated assassination plot involving cooperation from the chief priests and elders themselves.

The intensity of the conspiracy underlines just how much institutional hostility Paul faced — this isn't a mob's spontaneous anger, but a deliberate, sworn plan involving the highest religious authorities in Jerusalem.

chapters.title: Paul's Sister's Son
chapters.teaser: An unnamed young relative overhears the murder plot and becomes the one who saves Paul's life.
body: Paul's nephew — otherwise unmentioned anywhere in the New Testament — hears of the plot and reports it, and the chief captain responds with striking seriousness: nearly 470 soldiers, horsemen, and spearmen assigned to escort Paul safely to Caesarea by night (v.16-23).

It's a quiet reminder that providence in Acts often works through very ordinary means — an anonymous family member's overheard conversation, not a dramatic angelic rescue this time, becomes the pivot point that keeps Paul alive.

chapters.title: A Pestilent Fellow
chapters.teaser: A hired orator opens the prosecution's case with flattery aimed squarely at the Roman governor.
body: Tertullus, the prosecution's spokesman, opens with elaborate praise of Felix's rule bringing "great quietness" (v.2-4) before pivoting to the accusation: Paul is "a pestilent fellow... a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes" (v.5) who tried to "profane the temple."
The rhetorical strategy is transparent — buttering up the judge before making an emotionally loaded, somewhat vague accusation, a contrast that sets up Paul's far more measured and specific defense.

chapters.title: The Way They Call Heresy
chapters.teaser: Paul insists his faith is a fulfillment of Judaism, not a break from it.
body: Paul's defense reframes the whole dispute: "after the way which they call heresy, so worship I the God of my fathers, believing all things which are written in the law and in the prophets" (v.14) — insisting on continuity, not rupture, with the tradition he's accused of betraying.

The term "the Way" appears repeatedly throughout Acts as an early name for the Christian movement, and here Paul explicitly claims it as a faithful extension of Judaism's own hope, particularly "the resurrection of the dead" shared "by the just and unjust" (v.15).

chapters.title: A Conscience Void of Offence
chapters.teaser: Paul grounds his defense not in legal technicalities but in his own settled personal integrity.
body: "Herein do I exercise myself, to have always a conscience void of offence toward God, and toward men" (v.16) is offered almost as a summary standard for his whole life, not just a defense against this particular charge.

It's a claim that shifts the conversation from procedural questions of guilt or innocence toward the deeper, harder-to-fake matter of character — inviting scrutiny of the whole pattern of his life, not just this one incident.

chapters.title: Felix Trembled
chapters.teaser: A private conversation about ethics unsettles the governor more than the public trial did.
body: Called for privately, Paul reasons with Felix "of righteousness, temperance, and judgment to come" — and the effect is visceral: "Felix trembled, and answered, Go thy way for this time" (v.25).

It's a striking contrast to the earlier courtroom scene: formal accusations left Felix unmoved, but plain talk about moral accountability genuinely rattles him, even as he ultimately postpones any real response.

chapters.title: He Hoped for Money
chapters.teaser: Felix keeps Paul imprisoned for two years, motivated by bribery and political convenience rather than justice.
body: Felix's ongoing conversations with Paul are revealed to have an ulterior motive: "he hoped also that money should have been given him of Paul, that he might loose him" (v.26) — corruption hiding behind a veneer of judicial process.

When Felix is replaced by Festus two years later, he leaves Paul "bound" purely "willing to shew the Jews a pleasure" (v.27) — an unjust imprisonment extended for years, entirely for the sake of political convenience rather than any actual legal finding against Paul.

chapters.title: I Appeal Unto Caesar
chapters.teaser: Facing a rigged hearing, Paul invokes his citizenship to move his case to Rome's highest court.
body: Festus, wanting to please the Jewish leadership, proposes moving Paul's trial back to Jerusalem — the very place a murder plot against him had already been uncovered (v.9). Paul, recognizing the danger, exercises a citizen's ultimate legal right: "I appeal unto Caesar" (v.11).
It's a calculated, decisive move — not desperation, but a deliberate use of Roman law to escape a compromised local process and secure a hearing before the empire's highest authority instead.

chapters.title: Unto Caesar Shalt Thou Go
chapters.teaser: Festus's ruling makes Paul's journey to Rome legally irreversible.
body: "Hast thou appealed unto Caesar? unto Caesar shalt thou go" (v.12) settles the matter with Roman legal finality — once invoked, the appeal can't simply be withdrawn or overridden by local authorities.

The ruling quietly fulfills what's been building since chapter 19, when Paul first said "I must also see Rome," and what the Lord promised him directly in chapter 23: he would bear witness there too. The legal machinery of the empire, oddly, becomes the very mechanism carrying out that purpose.

chapters.title: One Jesus, Which Was Dead
chapters.teaser: Festus tries to summarize Paul's case to King Agrippa, and reveals he doesn't understand it at all.
body: Attempting to explain the charges to Agrippa, Festus stumbles through language that betrays total confusion: the dispute was about "their own superstition, and of one Jesus, which was dead, whom Paul affirmed to be alive" (v.19).
